question: The 8 recovery rows made the clone unsafe. If they count for less in training, does the clone stay safe and still learn something?
measure: Successes out of 3 from the normal start, and per-try safety counts: clipped frames (command cut at a joint limit), limited frames (cut by the speed limiter), unsafe-contact frames.
outcome: No weight worked. Weights 0.10 and 0.50 memorized the recording and failed 0/3 with clipping. Weight 0.25 missed the memorization bar and was not run. A new static safety check also failed the clone that has no recovery rows, so it was demoted to a log line.
setup: A policy is the network that drives the arm. The clone is a small network trained to copy a 450-step recording of the teacher, a script that cheats by reading the cube's true position. Experiment 03 added 8 recovery rows (the teacher's command after a small nudge) and the clone became unsafe. The loss is the number training pushes down: the average error over the rows. A loss weight scales how much one row counts; weight 0.10 means a recovery row counts a tenth as much as a normal row. The memorization bar is the offline gate: mean squared error (MSE) at most 1e-6 on the 450 normal rows. The static check scans the commands the model would give between recorded states and flags any that go out of bounds, without running the simulator.

parts.title: Is there a weight that keeps the normal start safe?
parts.why: If one weight works, use it. If none does, sparse recovery rows are a dead end.
parts.did: Retrained with the same 8 rows at weights 0.10, 0.25 and 0.50. Architecture, inputs, normalization, seed, optimizer, schedule, data, simulator and safety path were held fixed. Each model that passed the bar got 3 tries from the normal start.
parts.conclusion: All three weights are rejected. No candidate reached the wider five-start or handoff tests. Sparse recovery rows stop here.

parts.title: Can a static scan stand in for a simulator run as a safety check?
parts.why: A check that needs no rollout would be cheaper and could gate training.
parts.did: Ran the strict interpolated command-bound scan on the candidates and on the weight-0 control.
parts.conclusion: The weight-0 control also fails the scan, although in the simulator it had zero clipped, limited or unsafe frames. A check that fails the known-clean case cannot gate anything. It became telemetry, and a 3/3 run from the normal start in MuJoCo stayed the first safety check that means something.

trust.text: Only the weight changed between candidates; the 8 rows were reused unchanged.
The failures repeat exactly across the three tries.

These runs used MuJoCo 3.11.0 by accident (a stray pip install; the project pins 3.9.0). The reports were moved to a quarantine folder and the training was not re-run. The log says the conclusion did not depend on the exact counts.
One seed, three weights, normal start only. Simulation only.
The record's number "0/3 at every weight" is slightly off: weight 0.25 never ran in the simulator because it missed the offline bar.

meaning: This closed the sparse-recovery idea. The next branch asked whether the network was missing information rather than data (experiment 05).
lesson: If a dial does not fix the problem at any setting, the idea is wrong, not the setting. And test a checker on a known-good case before trusting it.

next.title: Add velocity, contact and history inputs (experiment 05)
next.why: Maybe the network cannot tell a recovery state from a normal one.

log:
**TL;DR:** Turning down the weight of the 8 recovery rows didn't help: every
version that trained still failed 0/3 on safety.

**Problem.** The 8 recovery rows broke the clone's safety (entry 03).

*How we know:* on the normal start, 291 clipped commands and 13 unsafe contacts
per try. I didn't know if a lighter touch would keep it safe while still
teaching something.

**Experiment.** Retrain with the same 8 rows counting 0.10, 0.25 and 0.50 as
much as a normal row in the loss, everything else frozen. I also wrote a static
check that scans the model's commands for anything out of bounds.

*What we hope to learn:* if one weight keeps the normal start safe, use it. If
none do, sparse recovery rows are a dead end.

**Outcome.** None worked:

| weight | memorization bar | normal start | per try |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.10 | passed | 0/3 | 119 clipped, 36 limited, 3 unsafe |
| 0.25 | missed | not run | |
| 0.50 | passed | 0/3 | 178 clipped, 175 limited |

- My static check was useless: even the model with no recovery rows at all
  failed it. Like a smoke alarm that goes off when you make toast. It became a
  log line, and a real 3/3 run in the sim became the first safety check I
  trusted.

*Note:* also run on the wrong MuJoCo version (entry 09), not re-run.

**Takeaway:** if a dial doesn't fix the problem at any setting, the idea is
wrong, not the setting. And test your checker on a known-good case before you
trust it.
